questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/52fc197612dac35373ecebf771b8444505902b5c6e00c7c55d2b21dab4809136.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $-4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/466c0aa389beb6d1a42092b73bae75508ef2c50f1f08cca5efaac20d25615f30.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4(1+2x).
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4(1+2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4(1+2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4(x+{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=-4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-4)^{2} & =4(1+{1}^{2})+C \\ 8 & =8+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+0 \\ {v}^{2} & =8(x+{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/3278eca2ae91f59c7c20d91f9190611291924dcc0cd6ffe74456552ba8400335.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-\sqrt{\pi }\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-\sqrt{\pi })^{2} & =-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+C \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+C \\ C & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ {v}^{2} & =2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2(\pi -2\operatorname{arctan}⁡3)} \\  & ≈-1.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $3\,m$ when its velocity is $2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/164c90893a07ae9657e90b6f2b25e53c9c4927b1f4a076429ba0521a98377f24.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {e}^{x-3}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={e}^{x-3}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=3\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & ={e}^{3-3}+C \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({e}^{x-3}+1) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ec4af1357e75dcee6d7d5412467c2ee2ea9e54fa38fb6e83817b0ae909c529aa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2+3{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x-3{e}^{-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2(0)-3{e}^{-0}+C \\ 2 & =-3+C \\ C & =2+3 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x-3{e}^{-x}+5 \\ {v}^{2} & =4x-6{e}^{-x}+10 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4(3)-6{e}^{-3}+10} \\ v & =\sqrt{22-6{e}^{-3}} \\ v & ≈4.7\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ad437638f22672a10a183f1521929637f8d43725f37a9736c569516232e7c468.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -2{e}^{-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2{e}^{0}+K \\ K & =2-2 \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ v & =\pm 2{e}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2{e}^{-x/2} \\ {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{x/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{x/2} & =t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{x/2}=t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/2} & =t+1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x/2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}\,m/s.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/2093298b6cacb0b29f874d401ccca40560517ff5887763e9a2b88bf4bc051abb.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)=\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}} \\ (1+x)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int (1+x)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int (1+x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}(1+x)^{3} & =t+K \\ (1+x)^{3} & =3t+C \\ 1+x & =\sqrt[3]{3t+C} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{3t+C}-1\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=\sqrt[3]{3t+1}-1.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ its acceleration is $2(x+2)^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t$ where $t\in [0,\frac{1}{4}].$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ba9988a12d1c70c43a6a010c3578850fe79a9bca01309884fe981b3f7cca512c.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2(x+2)^{3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2(x+2)^{3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2(x+2)^{3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2(x+2)^{3}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(0+2)^{4}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4} \\ {v}^{2} & =(x+2)^{4} \\ v & =\pm (x+2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(x+2)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 1\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{x+2} & =t+C \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =-t-C.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=-\frac{1}{2},$ and the particular solution is

$$
\frac{1}{x+2}=-t+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+2} & =-t+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =\frac{1-2t}{2} \\ x+2 & =\frac{2}{1-2t} \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-2t}-2 \\ x & =\frac{4t}{1-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ its acceleration is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/ee516744d915553bf962b498af522cf0006d42c5d0e0e2a003e6f385dd069e4a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8\sqrt{0+1}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =16\sqrt{x+1} \\ v & =\pm 4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4\sqrt[4]{x+1} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{4}{3}(x+1)^{3/4} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{3{C}_{1}}{4}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/4}=3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{4/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{4/3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=3x\,m/s.$ If $x=2\,m$ when $t=0,$ find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/efdb69673b4088d3c021d78282642ff7abc57158e23704cd3d5e7ff2559cbdbb.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)=3x.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3x.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3x \\ \frac{1}{3x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{3x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x| & =t+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|x| & =3t+3K \\ x & ={e}^{3t+3K} \\ x & =C{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=2$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=2,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=2{e}^{3t}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0$. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\, \rm{ m/s}$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $\sin^2 x \,\rm{m/s}^2.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ what differential equation describes this motion?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/f187eff194f136838b67ab12b44f8f6882eafb59885a5c3f440d41492def4a42.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\sin^2 x$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-{sin}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
v \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = -\sin^2 x.\qquad \qquad (\ast)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(v^2) = 2v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(\ast)$ as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = -\sin^2 x.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x \,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \, \rm{m/s}^2.$ If $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x = 1 \, \textrm m.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/4fdd70a4ca80965c0adce9c60be36b0712852b662cff69f9733f50c739fd1b32.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x-2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = x^2 + e^{x-2} + C.
$$

Now, since $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2}+{e}^{2-2}+C \\ 8 & =4+1+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v = \sqrt{2\left(x^2 + e^{x-2} + 3\right)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x = 1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({1}^{2}+{e}^{1-2}+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(4+{e}^{-1})} \\  & ≈2.96\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\geq 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\textrm m,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/eca36626e6a0cfb30d293e684483c37ddce6f18d4004c3f77258e9663565d8d7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\, \textrm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{2}{0+1}+K \\ 2 & =2+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{4}{x+1} \\ v & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x) > 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1)^{3/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = \dfrac{3C_1}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/2} =3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{2/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{2/3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$
